title: Not the thing, my view
hook: if something outside pains you, it's your judgment of it, and that you can change (Meditations 8.47)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chickpea in the pot, and the cook who said the heat was making it good. Your line was being cooked. Did you stay in the pot a little longer? Day two hundred eight.

It's raining on the day of the picnic. One person says: great, ruined. Another says: fine, we'll eat in the car, it'll be an adventure. Same rain. Same car. Or two people get the same curt email from the boss. One spends the evening furious. The other shrugs: she's probably slammed this week. The email didn't change. What changed was the story each of them told about it. Marcus kept coming back, in his notebook, to that gap between what happens and what we make of it. Today: not the thing, my view.
screen: `SAME RAIN, TWO PICNICS.` → `THE STORY WE TELL ABOUT IT.` → `NOT THE THING, MY VIEW.`

segments.voice: Here's how Book Eight, section forty-seven, begins in George Long's translation: "If thou art pained by any external thing, it is not this thing that disturbs thee, but thy own judgment about it." And then: it's in your power to wipe out that judgment now. It's an old Stoic idea. Marcus had read Epictetus, the former slave turned teacher, and Epictetus said something very close: people are troubled not by things, but by their opinions about things. Now, let's be fair to the idea, because it's easy to hear it wrong. Marcus isn't saying pain is imaginary. A broken arm hurts. Grief is real. What he's pointing at is the second layer: the story on top. This shouldn't be happening. This always happens to me. This is a disaster. That layer is judgment, and judgment is yours to examine. And Marcus goes further in the same passage. If what bothers you is something in your own character, who's stopping you from correcting it? And if it's that you're not doing something you know is right, why not do it instead of complaining? And if something too strong for you really stands in the way, then don't grieve, because the cause isn't yours. So this isn't just changing your mind. It's a sorting. Some things you reframe. Some you act on. Some you let go. What you can almost always do is notice the story and ask whether it's true. Your line: not the thing, my view.
screen: `IT IS NOT THIS THING THAT DISTURBS THEE.` · `EPICTETUS: NOT THINGS, BUT OPINIONS.` · `REFRAME, ACT, OR LET GO.` · then, large: `NOT THE THING, MY VIEW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rephrase one complaint. Settle, and let one small complaint come up. The traffic, a coworker, the weather. Say it inside the way you usually do. Then say it again, plainly, without the story: what actually happened? Then notice the judgment you added, and ask if it's true. Try one new sentence about it. The bell holds the time.
Epictetus, the former slave and teacher Marcus read: people are troubled not by things but by their opinions about them. Today's word.
Your line: the story on top. Today, catch one complaint as it comes out of your mouth, and rephrase it once. Day two hundred eight.

howItsDone: Readers of the Stoics often practice separating events from judgments, sometimes by writing down what happened and then the story they told about it; modern cognitive therapy draws on a similar idea.

original.note: Greek: a judgment, an assumption, one's take on a thing. Marcus uses it elsewhere in the notebook for the view we add to events.

trapdoor: what you thought: just think positive.
what it means: the thing is one layer; your judgment about it is another, and that one is yours to examine.
what a scholar hears: the Stoic line between what happens and the judgment we add to it, voiced in Epictetus's Handbook, section five, and echoed in Marcus's own notes.

sources.quoted: If thou art pained by any external thing, it is not this thing that disturbs thee, but thy own judgment about it.

notes: Confirm the Long 1862 wording of 8.47's first sentence exactly. The Project Gutenberg text of Long (ebook 15877) reads 'judgment'; the quotation now follows it.
Rest of 8.47 paraphrased: wiping out the judgment, correcting one's own disposition, acting rather than complaining, not grieving when the cause lies outside one's power. Confirm.
Epictetus, Enchiridion 5, paraphrased rather than quoted from Long 1877.

Softened 'Marcus learned it from Epictetus' to 'Marcus had read Epictetus' (teach and myth game): Marcus credits Rusticus with lending him Epictetus's discourses (Meditations 1.7), but how directly his thought derives from Epictetus is a matter of scholarly discussion. Confirm phrasing.
Trapdoor softened: it no longer attributes the impression/assent distinction specifically to Handbook 5 (that section is about opinions; assent is developed elsewhere in Epictetus). Confirm.
howItsDone mentions cognitive therapy drawing on a similar idea; this is widely stated by CBT's founders. Confirm.

Editor review 2026-10-01: quotation of 8.47 matched to the Gutenberg text of Long ('judgment'); cut the unsourced 'Marcus spent his life', 'the heart of Stoic practice' and 'which people often skip'. The Greek in 8.47 itself is krima (κρίμα), not hypolepsis; the original-word note now says Marcus uses ὑπόληψις elsewhere. Keeper may prefer κρίμα.
